title: Cucumber Sandwich
subtitle: Thin-sliced cucumber in buttered white bread with cream cheese
excerpt: Paper-thin cucumber slices on buttered white bread with cream cheese, lightly seasoned. The British afternoon tea sandwich: delicate, cold, and satisfying.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Cucumber sandwiches as a standard for afternoon tea and garden parties. Isabella Beeton's original version used buttered bread only, without cream cheese. The cream cheese addition became common in the twentieth century. Agnes Jekyll, Kitchen Essays (1922), cucumber sandwiches as essential for summer garden parties.

recipe.batchNotes: Make many batches easily. Keep covered with a damp cloth in the fridge for up to 2 hours before serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Salt the cucumber 15 minutes before assembling to draw out excess water. Assemble up to 2 hours ahead and keep covered in the fridge.

content.text: Cucumber sandwiches depend entirely on execution. The cucumber must be sliced thin enough to be almost transparent. The bread must be fresh and lightly but evenly buttered. The crusts must be removed. The result is a cool, restrained mouthful that is exactly the right thing to eat with a pot of tea in the middle of the afternoon.
Salting the cucumber briefly draws out excess water and prevents the bread from going soggy. 10 minutes is enough. Pat thoroughly dry before using.

items.prepNote: sliced as thinly as possible, ideally on a mandoline
thin slices, crusts removed after assembly
a pinch for salting the cucumber
finely snipped, optional addition to the cream cheese

content.text: Slice {{cucumber}} cucumber as thinly as possible. Lay on a plate, sprinkle lightly with salt, and leave for 10 minutes. Pat completely dry with kitchen paper.
Soften {{cream-cheese}} of cream cheese and mix with chives if using. Season with a small pinch of white pepper.
Spread {{salted-butter}} of softened butter thinly on one side of each slice of {{bread-white}} bread. Spread the cream cheese on the buttered side of two slices.
Layer the dried cucumber slices over the cream cheese in overlapping rows. Close with the second buttered slice and press lightly.
Trim the crusts with a sharp knife. Cut each sandwich into 3 equal fingers or 4 triangles. Arrange on a plate and serve cold.

rows.symptom: Bread is soggy by the time the sandwiches are served
rows.cause: Cucumber not dried properly after salting, or assembled too far ahead
rows.fix: Pat the cucumber very dry and assemble no more than 2 hours before serving. Keep covered with a damp cloth or cling film in the fridge.

rows.symptom: Cucumber slices are thick and crunchy rather than delicate
rows.cause: No mandoline used, or knife not sharp enough
rows.fix: Use a sharp knife or a mandoline set to 2 mm. The cucumber should be nearly translucent.

rows.symptom: Bread tears when trimming the crusts
rows.cause: Knife not sharp enough or sandwich not pressed together firmly first
rows.fix: Press the sandwich together firmly before cutting. Use a serrated bread knife or a very sharp chef's knife.

rows.symptom: Cream cheese is too thick and hard to spread
rows.fix: Let it sit at room temperature for 20 minutes before using. It should spread as easily as butter.

content.text: The cucumber sandwich is the defining item of British afternoon tea. It became a shorthand for refinement and restraint. Oscar Wilde used it as comic punctuation in The Importance of Being Earnest. It has appeared in nearly every satire of English upper-class manners since. You find it at Wimbledon, at Buckingham Palace garden parties, and at village fetes across England.
